title: Explain Master-Slave architecture, its use cases, and what happens if the master or a slave dies.
shortTitle: Explain Master-Slave architecture, its use cases, and what happens if the master or a slave dies
keyPoints: One primary (master) takes all writes and replicates to replicas (slaves) that serve reads.
Replication can be async (fast but risk of data loss) or sync (safe but adds write latency).
A dead replica just loses read capacity with no data loss; reads shift to other replicas.
A dead primary halts writes until a replica is promoted, risking loss of not-yet-replicated writes.
Split-brain is the danger: two nodes both think they are primary and accept conflicting writes.
Replication lag creates eventual consistency on reads; route fresh reads to the primary.
Primary-replica scales reads but not writes; for write scalability, you need sharding.

s1_definition.oneliner: One primary takes all writes as the source of truth and replicates to replicas that serve reads; a dead replica just loses read capacity, but a dead primary halts writes until a replica is promoted.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Primary (master)** – The single node that accepts all writes and is the authoritative source of truth.
- **Replica (slave)** – One or more nodes that receive a continuous copy of the primary's data and serve read traffic.
- **Async replication** – Primary commits and acknowledges immediately, ships changes afterward; fast but risks losing recent writes on primary failure.
- **Sync replication** – Primary waits for at least one replica to confirm before acknowledging; safe but adds write latency.
- **Failover** – Promoting a replica to primary when the old primary fails; can be manual or automated.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps one official master ledger that only the head cashier can write to. Several assistants keep photocopies and serve customers who just want to read their balance. If one assistant is off sick, customers ask another. But if the head cashier suddenly leaves, nobody can record new transactions until one assistant is promoted, and any entry the cashier had written but not yet shared could be lost.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Primary-Replica Architecture:

  Write Path:
  Client ──▶ Primary ──▶ Commit ──▶ Replicate
                                      │
                          ┌───────────┼───────────┐
                          ▼           ▼           ▼
                     Replica-1   Replica-2   Replica-3

  Read Path:
  Client ──▶ Load Balancer ──▶ Replica-1 (or 2 or 3)

  Failure Scenarios:
  Replica dies:  Read traffic shifts. No data loss. Writes unaffected.
  Primary dies:  Writes STOP. Promote replica. Risk: data loss + split-brain.

  Failover:
  ┌─────────┐  dead  ┌──────────────┐  promote  ┌───────────────┐
  │ Primary │───────▶│ Failover     │──────────▶│ Replica-1     │
  │ (dead)  │        │ Controller   │           │ (new Primary) │
  └─────────┘        │ (detects,    │           └───────────────┘
                     │  selects,    │
                     │  fences old) │
                     └──────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Primary-replica is a replication architecture with one authoritative writer and multiple read copies. All writes go to the primary, which records them in a replication log. Replicas receive the stream of changes and serve read traffic. This scales reads, provides high availability, and enables backups and analytics without burdening the primary.

The failure scenarios are asymmetric. A dead replica is graceful: reads shift to others, no data loss, writes unaffected, and the repaired replica catches up. A dead primary is serious: writes stop, reads grow stale, and recovery means promoting the most up-to-date replica. The risks are data loss (writes committed but not yet replicated) and split-brain (two nodes both acting as primary), which robust failover prevents with quorum and fencing.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj moved all reads to replicas to relieve an overloaded database. When a replica crashed, there was no impact. When the primary failed, they promoted a replica within 30 seconds, losing only the last few uncommitted writes. For critical data they switched to semi-sync replication so an acknowledged write was guaranteed to survive a primary failure. The key limitation is that primary-replica scales reads but not writes.

Remember one sentence: one primary takes all writes and replicates to replicas for read scaling and availability; a dead replica just loses read capacity, while a dead primary halts writes until promoted, risking loss of not-yet-replicated writes.
